Messages.Author: Tammy, Chris, and Alex Shorb
Messages.Body:
Got some Q's about the tourney rules.

-----
1.4. Taking Notes
Players are not allowed to take written notes of their opponents'
decks or activities, with the exception of the following items:

Their opponents' names (and other relevant personal information)
Their opponents' V:EKN numbers
Which player played first.
Status of the game (such as counters in pool, Master: Out-of-Turn
cards played, transfers taken, diableries made, resources, and so on)
The number of turns that have elapsed.
-----

Can you take notes about your own play?

-----
3.6. Conceding Games
Players may concede a game at any time provided all but one of the
players agree to concede, with the result that game is recorded as if
the remaining player had succeeded in ousting the conceding players in
sequence. Please note that players who attempt to bribe, coerce, or
otherwise improperly induce their opponents to concede will be subject
to the appropriate section of the V:EKN Penalty Guidelines.
-----

This makes it sound like you must have exactly one dissenter. If it
is unanimous, then the player's can't concede. I know you mean that
all but one of the players concedes, and all players must agree to it,
but it does not exactly read that way. Perhaps change "provided all
but one of the players agree to concede" to "provided all players
agree on which player does not concede" or something.

I notice that the blood counting tie-breaker has been removed, at
least form section 3 - reasoning? I have been in tournaments wherein
the blood tie-breaker was not enough and a die had to be rolled...

-----
4.4. Card Elevation and Disposition
Players must keep their cards above the level of the playing surface.
Revealing cards in your hand or uncontrolled area to an opponent is
not allowed.
-----

Even when trying to make a deal? Can you reveal a card to everyone in
that situation?

Thanks,

Chris
--

Alexander Shorb 2'10"
Chris Shorb 5'11"

As I understood the V:TES collusion rule, you could not enter into a
deal with another player so as to make yourself not gain a victory
point. You can make deals that give others a (short-term) advantage,
but you can't make a deal that would lead to your ousting. I.e., I
cannot make a deal with another player (who might be my buddy who I am
going to split the prizes with later) to give her all my pool via
Succubus Club.

The consession rule as you have it here makes it sound like you can do
exactly that, and without even having to use an in-game mechanic.

> > > > I notice that the blood counting tie-breaker has been removed, at
> > > > least form section 3 - reasoning? I have been in tournaments wherein
> > > > the blood tie-breaker was not enough and a die had to be rolled...
> > >

> > > unduly increases the recordkeeping duties.
> >
> > So what do we do about breaking ties of VP and TP then? Rolling a die
>
> Yes, rolling a die (or flipping a coin or whatever).
>

I don't really get this - please explain how rolling a die is more or
equally a measure of performance compared to blood. Your total blood
count on your vamps and in your pool I think relates directly to your
power during a game.

Was there cheating involved with people overcounting their blood? Or
perhaps forgetting to count their blood? Are there concerns about
folks pumping up their blood count when their prey is totally
helpless, in order to gain a competetive advantage? The final one
here still sounds like a true measure of performance...

Chris

The "inevitable coin toss" is not as inevitable if you use a tertiary
tie-breaker.

>

> > perhaps forgetting to count their blood? Are there concerns about
> > folks pumping up their blood count when their prey is totally
> > helpless, in order to gain a competetive advantage? The final one
> > here still sounds like a true measure of performance...
>
> A measure of some performance, but not of winning.

Aha. You win a single game with Victory points, and that is the only
way you win. If the VP are tied, then the game is a tie game
(although we play a house rule that whoever is standing at the end, in
the case of tie is the winner). To determine a series of games, you
total VP. Since in tournament play you can't have a tie, the table
point system was created. VP also determines your table points. The
gradation of table points is arbitrary (they could have used 10, 20,
30, 40, 50 or 1,2,pi, 4, 5), but it still is directly tied to VP.
There are really no other meaningful measures of how victorious you
were than VP, and directly tied to VP, TP.

But tournaments (and competition in general) are also about the thrill
of victory and the agony of defeat. It seems to go against that tenet
that after 2-3 preliminary rounds of grueling play, who gets into the
finals is decided by a coin toss. I like Noal's suggestion that a
final can be a 6 player game. I wonder though how that would effect
ratings. I would also suggest that if the final winner is also tied
(2VP each, w/ equal VP & TP from earlier rounds), they have a duel to
determine a winner. At least the tournament is decided "on the field"
and not by coin flip.

Although I'm loathe to suggest it, play ratings might be an adequate
measurement of this. In the case of a tie, add up the player ratings of
the people they ousted. The highest total wins.

An alternate possibility, albeit a much poorer one, IMO, would be that
the player with the highest rating wins ties. It would be the best
incentive to increase your rating that I've heard to date.

Play a quick VTES *duel* between the two tied players! Both players
start with 15 pool, and no pool can be gained during that "mini-game".
I don't think a tie can be resolved any directer. :)

Well, it's a bit weird, but it just sprang to my mind. :)

Carl

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
You know, the more that I think about it this topic, the more certain I am that
there is no *real* way we can solve this problem.

What I mean is, to a large degree, there is no "fairer" way.

We've heard about the possibility of using sweeps, and how it might be unfair
since one might simply get "lucky" or be at a table with unskilled players.

We've heard about why we should (or shouldn't) use pool to determine the
winner.

Someone has also suggested playing a mini-game, which in itself has its own
problems since one on one games are drastically different from multi-player
games.

In the end, maybe we should just go with the coin toss. Everything has its pros
and cons, so why NOT just leave it to chance. The other solutions are biased
towards certain decks (decks that have an all or nothing mentality, massive
pool gain decks, and combat or other decks that do well one on one). At least
the coin toss is unbiased (more or less). I was originally very opposed to
leaving the victory to chance, but I'm beginning to not care so much
anymore....

Halcyan 2

Messages.Body:
i don't normally read the newsgroup, but anthony, who is notorious for
getting others to do stuff for him, has asked me to mention a method
that those of us who play in canberra seem to agree is a fair method of
breaking ties.

we call them Ousting Points. they're like the 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 of
tournament points, but they are allocated when you are ousted. if you
are the first player ousted, you get 12. 2nd player ousted gets 24. etc.
last player standing gets 60. if more than one player is ousted
simultaneously, the points are split (like TPs). if more than one player
survives the round (due to time lapse), the remaining points are split.
it's worked well, and is tied to performance.

although the performance it is related to isn't directly how well you
oust people, there is a tendancy for those that oust people well to
be less likely to be ousted themselves before others (due to their deck
ousting others' faster, and/or gaining 6 pool when they do out someone).

i think it's at least well worth considering as an option. in my mind it
is FAR superior to a random event.
